blocks.html: The quantum numbers label one electron's states. Atoms with many electrons need one more rule, found by Wolfgang Pauli in 1925, and it is the reason chemistry exists: without it, every electron would drop into the 1s state and all atoms would act alike.

The exclusion principle: no two electrons in an atom can have the same four quantum numbers $(n, l, m_l, m_s)$. So each orbital $(n, l, m_l)$ holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins. Electrons fill the lowest available states first (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, …), and the outermost electrons set an element's chemistry. Electron spin is an intrinsic angular momentum with $|S| = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hbar$ and $S_z = \pm\frac{1}{2}\hbar$.

Spin was discovered in experiments. In 1922 Otto Stern and Walther Gerlach sent silver atoms through a non-uniform magnetic field, and the beam split cleanly into two spots, not a smear: a magnetic moment that takes only two orientations. Spin is not a tiny ball turning: an electron behaves as a point particle in every experiment so far, and a ball small enough to match would need its surface to move faster than light to carry that much angular momentum. Spin is simply a built-in property, like charge. The exclusion principle then builds the periodic table: each new element adds one electron in the lowest open state, so shells fill in turn, and elements whose outer subshells are filled alike (like lithium, sodium and potassium, each with one s electron outside a closed shell) behave alike.

blocks.html: Thinking spin means the electron is a tiny ball literally turning. The name is historical. Spin acts like angular momentum (it adds to orbital angular momentum and gives the electron a magnetic moment), but it takes exactly two values and has nothing to do with the electron's size. A check: a classical spinning ball could spin at any rate; the electron's spin is always $\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\hbar$.

blocks.html: One atom has sharp energy levels. Bring two atoms together and each level splits in two; bring $10^{23}$ together in a crystal and each level spreads into a nearly continuous band of allowed energies, separated by gaps with no states at all. The exclusion principle then fills the bands from the bottom, two electrons per state, and how the filling ends decides whether a solid is a metal, an insulator or a semiconductor.

• Conductor: the highest occupied band is only partly filled, so electrons can move into nearby empty states and carry current.
  • Insulator: the highest filled band (valence band) is full and a wide gap (several eV; diamond's is 5.5 eV) separates it from the empty conduction band.
  • Semiconductor: the same picture with a small gap (silicon 1.12 eV, germanium 0.67 eV), so heat or light lifts some electrons across, and conduction rises steeply with temperature.
A photon can move an electron across the gap only if $hf \ge E_g$; an LED emits light with $hf \approx E_g$.

In a full band, every state is taken, so an electric field can't shift electrons into states of different momentum: no net current. Conduction needs empty states just above the filled ones. In a metal they are right there. In a semiconductor, an electron needs about $E_g$ to reach them, and at temperature $T$ the chance of having that much thermal energy goes roughly like $e^{-E_g/2k_BT}$ for the number of electrons that make it across. That factor grows fast with $T$, which is why warming a semiconductor lowers its resistance, while a metal's resistance rises (its electron count is fixed, and hotter atoms scatter them more). Doping adds carriers on purpose: a phosphorus atom (5 outer electrons) in silicon (4) donates an electron (n-type); a boron atom (3) leaves a hole (p-type).

blocks.html: In Physics 2 you saw that a nucleus weighs less than the protons and neutrons it is made of, and that the missing mass, times $c^2$, is its binding energy. Here we look at the whole family of nuclei: how big they are, and which ones are held most tightly. The answer explains why the Sun shines by fusing light nuclei and why reactors run by splitting heavy ones.

A nucleus with $A$ nucleons has radius $$R = r_0A^{1/3},\qquad r_0 \approx 1.2\ \text{fm}\ (1\ \text{fm} = 10^{-15}\ \text{m}),$$ so every nucleus has about the same density, $2.3 \times 10^{17}$ kg/m³. Its binding energy, from atomic masses, is $$E_B = \left[Zm(^1\text{H}) + Nm_n - M(^A\text{X})\right]c^2,\qquad 1\ \text{u}\cdot c^2 = 931.5\ \text{MeV}.$$ The binding energy per nucleon, $E_B/A$, rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks near iron and nickel at about 8.8 MeV, and falls slowly for heavy nuclei.

If nucleons pack together like marbles, each taking the same volume, the nucleus's volume is proportional to $A$, and its radius to $A^{1/3}$. Constant density means the strong force holds each nucleon to its near neighbors only (it has a short range). That explains the shape of the curve. A nucleon inside a big nucleus has a full set of neighbors, but in a small nucleus many nucleons sit at the surface with fewer neighbors, so light nuclei are loosely bound. Protons also repel each other electrically, and that repulsion reaches across the whole nucleus, growing roughly like $Z^2$; in heavy nuclei it wins back some of the binding. The best compromise is near $A \approx 56$ to 62. Using atomic masses (with $^1$H, not a bare proton) keeps the electrons balanced: $Z$ hydrogen atoms bring the same $Z$ electrons as the neutral atom.

blocks.html: In Chemistry you used half-lives: after each one, half of the remaining nuclei are left. Calculus shows why the pattern is exponential, and it adds two useful quantities: the decay constant and the activity. The key fact is that a nucleus has no memory: an old uranium nucleus is exactly as likely to decay in the next second as a new one.

Each nucleus decays with the same probability $\lambda\,dt$ in a short time $dt$, so $$\frac{dN}{dt} = -\lambda N \quad\Longrightarrow\quad N(t) = N_0e^{-\lambda t}.$$ The half-life is $T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$, the mean life is $\tau = \frac{1}{\lambda}$, and the activity (decays per second, in becquerels, Bq) is $$A = \lambda N = A_0e^{-\lambda t}.$$

With $N$ nuclei, each decaying with probability $\lambda\,dt$, the expected number of decays in $dt$ is $\lambda N\,dt$, so $dN = -\lambda N\,dt$. Separate the variables: $\frac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\,dt$, so $\ln N = -\lambda t + C$ and $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, the exponential whose derivative is proportional to itself. The half-life comes from $\frac{1}{2} = e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}}$: take logs, $T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$. A big $\lambda$ means a short half-life: they are inverses, not the same thing. And the activity is the decay rate, $-\frac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$: a sample with many nuclei but a long half-life can have a small activity.

blocks.html: Every nuclear reaction and decay either releases energy or needs it. The binding energies tell you roughly which way it goes, but the exact bookkeeping is simpler: compare the total mass before with the total mass after.

The Q-value of a reaction or decay is $$Q = \left(\sum m_{\text{before}} - \sum m_{\text{after}}\right)c^2,\qquad 1\ \text{u}\cdot c^2 = 931.5\ \text{MeV}.$$ $Q > 0$: energy is released (as kinetic energy of the products and gamma rays). $Q < 0$: energy must be supplied. Using atomic masses, the electrons cancel in alpha decay, beta-minus decay and most reactions; for beta-plus decay, subtract $2m_ec^2 = 1.022$ MeV.

Total energy, including rest energy, is conserved. If the products have less rest mass, the difference has become kinetic energy. Tables list masses of neutral atoms, which include electrons. In alpha decay, $^{238}$U (92 electrons) becomes $^{234}$Th (90 electrons) plus $^4$He (2 electrons): the electrons balance. In beta-minus decay the nucleus gains a proton and emits an electron, and the daughter atom needs one more electron: again they balance. In beta-plus decay the nucleus loses a proton and emits a positron; the daughter atom has one electron too many, and a positron leaves as well, so the atomic masses miss two electron masses: $Q = [M_{\text{parent}} - M_{\text{daughter}} - 2m_e]c^2$.

blocks.html: The decay law turns a radioactive isotope into a clock. If you know how much of a parent isotope a sample started with, and how much is left, the exponential gives the time that has passed. Two clocks cover most of history: carbon-14 for things that were alive in the last few tens of thousands of years, and uranium–lead for rocks billions of years old. Try it in the Science Lab's Build an Atom, where half-lives date ancient wood and bone.

From $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, the age is $$t = \frac{T_{1/2}}{\ln 2}\,\ln\frac{N_0}{N}.$$ Carbon-14 ($T_{1/2} = 5730$ yr): living things keep the same $^{14}$C share as the air; after death it decays, giving ages up to about 50,000 years. Uranium–lead ($^{238}$U → $^{206}$Pb, $T_{1/2} = 4.47 \times 10^9$ yr): if a mineral started with no lead and kept every atom, $N_0 = N_{\text{U}} + N_{\text{Pb}}$, so $$t = \frac{T_{1/2}}{\ln 2}\,\ln\left(1 + \frac{N_{\text{Pb}}}{N_{\text{U}}}\right).$$

Take logarithms of $\frac{N}{N_0} = e^{-\lambda t}$ (solving exponential equations): $\ln\frac{N_0}{N} = \lambda t$, and $\lambda = \frac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$. The clock's useful range is set by the half-life. After about 9 half-lives (50,000 years for carbon-14), less than 0.2% of the original remains, too little to measure against background; for a clock to read billions of years, it needs a half-life in the billions. In the uranium–lead method, each decayed uranium atom becomes a lead atom (through a chain of short-lived steps), so the lead counts the decays. Zircon crystals are ideal: they take in uranium but reject lead when they form.

blocks.html: Inside the nucleus are protons and neutrons, and for decades they looked fundamental. Then accelerators produced hundreds of new short-lived particles, and in 1964 Murray Gell-Mann and George Zweig proposed that most of them, protons and neutrons included, are built from a few smaller pieces: quarks. Experiments at SLAC in 1968, firing electrons into protons, found hard, point-like bits inside, just as Rutherford had found the nucleus inside the atom.

Matter is built from two families of fundamental particles, each with an antiparticle:
  • Leptons (not made of anything smaller): the electron, muon and tau, each with its neutrino.
  • Quarks: up $(+\frac{2}{3}e)$, down $(-\frac{1}{3}e)$, strange $(-\frac{1}{3}e)$, charm $(+\frac{2}{3}e)$, bottom $(-\frac{1}{3}e)$, top $(+\frac{2}{3}e)$.
Quarks are always bound into hadrons: baryons hold three quarks (proton $uud$, neutron $udd$), and mesons hold a quark and an antiquark (the pion $\pi^+ = u\bar{d}$).

Quark charges are fractions, yet every particle ever observed has a whole-number charge. The rule that explains it is color: each quark carries one of three “color” charges of the strong force, and only color-neutral combinations can exist on their own: three quarks with one of each color, or a quark with an antiquark carrying its anticolor. Check the charges: $uud$ gives $\frac{2}{3} + \frac{2}{3} - \frac{1}{3} = +1$, and $udd$ gives $0$. Pulling a quark out of a hadron takes so much energy that new quark–antiquark pairs form first (confinement), so no lone quark has ever been seen. Each quark has baryon number $\frac{1}{3}$, which is why every baryon has $B = 1$ and every meson $B = 0$.

blocks.html: Thinking protons and neutrons are fundamental particles. Each is three quarks held together by the strong force, and its mass comes mostly from the energy of that binding, not from the quarks' own small masses. The electron, by contrast, really does seem fundamental: no experiment has found any size or structure in it. A quick check: if the proton were fundamental, the neutron (with no charge) and the proton (charge $+1$) would have no reason to be so similar in mass.

blocks.html: Every particle has an antiparticle with the same mass and opposite charge. Paul Dirac's 1928 relativistic equation for the electron implied that it must have a partner, and in 1932 Carl Anderson found it, the positron, in cosmic-ray tracks. When matter meets its antimatter, both can vanish into pure energy, and energy can make new pairs. Relativistic energy and momentum decide exactly when.

Pair production: a photon near a nucleus can become a particle–antiparticle pair if its energy is at least $$E_\gamma \ge 2mc^2\qquad(1.022\ \text{MeV for an electron–positron pair}).$$ Annihilation: an electron and a positron at rest turn into (at least) two photons of $m_ec^2 = 0.511$ MeV each, flying in opposite directions. A single photon cannot make a pair in empty space, and a pair at rest cannot make a single photon: momentum would not be conserved.

Conservation of energy says the photon must supply at least the two rest energies, $2mc^2$. Momentum is the subtle part. A photon with energy $E$ carries momentum $p = E/c$. A pair with that total momentum has energy at least $\sqrt{(pc)^2 + (2mc^2)^2}$, which is always more than $pc$. So a lone photon in empty space never has enough energy for its momentum. Near a nucleus, the nucleus absorbs some momentum (taking almost no energy, since it is heavy), and the pair can form. For annihilation at rest, the total momentum is zero; one photon always has momentum, so at least two photons must come out, back to back, sharing the energy equally.

blocks.html: Particles change into other particles all the time: neutrons decay, pions decay, collisions in accelerators make showers of new particles. Some changes never happen, though, even when charge balances. A handful of conservation laws, found by watching which reactions occur and which don't, sorts the allowed from the forbidden. They build on particle families.

In every reaction and decay, these totals are the same before and after:
  • electric charge $Q$;
  • baryon number $B$ ($+1$ for baryons, $-1$ for antibaryons, $\frac{1}{3}$ per quark, 0 for mesons and leptons);
  • lepton numbers $L_e$, $L_\mu$, $L_\tau$, separately ($+1$ for each lepton of that family and its neutrino, $-1$ for their antiparticles);
  • energy and momentum (a particle at rest can only decay into lighter particles).
Strangeness is conserved by the strong and electromagnetic forces but can change by 1 in weak decays.

These laws are summaries of experiments, and they are very well tested. Baryon number explains why the proton, the lightest baryon, does not decay: there is no lighter baryon for it to become. Experiments watching enormous tanks of water have found no proton decay at all, putting its lifetime beyond about $10^{34}$ years. Lepton numbers explain the neutrinos' bookkeeping: in neutron decay, $n \to p + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e$, the electron has $L_e = +1$, so an antineutrino with $L_e = -1$ must come out with it. Without that antineutrino, energy and momentum would not balance either; that is how Wolfgang Pauli predicted the neutrino in 1930, decades before it was detected.

blocks.html: Everything that happens in nature comes down to four interactions. Gravity and electromagnetism you know well. The other two act only inside nuclei and particles. In the modern picture, each force (except, so far, gravity) works by trading carrier particles, and the mass of the carrier sets how far the force reaches. This connects back to the particle families.

• Strong: binds quarks into protons, neutrons and other hadrons, carried by gluons; between nucleons it appears as the short-range nuclear force (range about 1 fm). Acts only on quarks and gluons, not on leptons.
  • Electromagnetic: acts on charges, carried by photons; infinite range.
  • Weak: changes one kind of quark or lepton into another (beta decay), carried by the heavy W⁺, W⁻ and Z⁰ bosons; range about $10^{-18}$ m.
  • Gravity: acts on all mass and energy; infinite range; far the weakest between particles. A carrier (the graviton) is proposed but not observed.

Why does a heavy carrier mean a short range? A carrier of mass $m$ appears out of nothing for a moment, so energy is “borrowed” by about $\Delta E = mc^2$. The uncertainty relation lets that last only about $\Delta t \approx \frac{\hbar}{mc^2}$, and in that time the carrier can travel at most about $c\,\Delta t$: $$R \approx \frac{\hbar}{mc} = \frac{\hbar c}{mc^2},\qquad \hbar c = 197.3\ \text{MeV·fm}.$$ This is Hideki Yukawa's 1935 argument: a nuclear force of range 1.4 fm needs a carrier of about 140 MeV, and the pion was found with just that mass. Massless photons give an infinite range. The W boson, at 80.4 GeV, gives about $2.5 \times 10^{-3}$ fm, which is why the weak force is so feeble at ordinary distances.
